PRE-EMPLOYMENT AND WORKPLACE DRUG TESTING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Morgan T. Ellis · Acme Manufacturing, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's constitutional and statutory framework governing drug testing of job applicants and employees at Acme Manufacturing, Inc. It states facts about what California law permits, requires, and restricts in this area. It is not itself a consent form, a drug-testing policy, or an authorization to test Morgan T. Ellis or anyone else, and it does not tell Morgan T. Ellis or Acme Manufacturing, Inc. what to do about any particular testing decision.

CALIFORNIA'S CONSTITUTIONAL RIGHT TO PRIVACY
California's Constitution states a specific, freestanding right to privacy. Article I, Section 1 lists privacy among the state's inalienable rights, alongside life, liberty, and property — an explicit textual right, not one inferred from other constitutional provisions the way many federal and state privacy protections are. California courts have applied this provision to drug testing in the employment context, discussed in the clauses that follow.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "All people are by nature free and independent and have inalienable rights. Among these are enjoying and defending life and liberty, acquiring, possessing, and protecting property, and pursuing and obtaining safety, happiness, and privacy."
  — Cal. Const. art. I, § 1 (California Legislative Information text), California Constitution, Declaration of Rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division=&title=&part=&chapter=&article=I)
  Known gap: This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Most other states' constitutions don't contain an explicit, freestanding privacy right at this level; where a privacy protection exists in another state, it more often comes from case law interpreting other constitutional text, federal constitutional doctrine, or statute. This clause states only the text of the provision itself — how California courts have applied it specifically to drug testing is addressed in the clauses that follow, not this one. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program.

THIS CONSTITUTIONAL PRIVACY RIGHT REACHES PRIVATE EMPLOYERS
In Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. (1994), the California Supreme Court held that Article I, Section 1's privacy provision protects individuals against invasions by private parties, not only against government action — the point a concurring and dissenting justice in the case described this way: he concurred "in the majority's initial conclusion that the privacy provision of article I, section 1, of the California Constitution affords protection to individuals with respect to the actions of a private entity, such as the National Collegiate Athletic Association (hereinafter NCAA)". This is the reason a private employer's drug-testing program in California can be challenged under this state constitutional privacy right at all, not only under a statute — most constitutional rights restrain only government action, and this is a specific, established exception.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "I concur in the majority’s initial conclusion that the privacy provision of article I, section 1, of the California Constitution affords protection to individuals with respect to the actions of a private entity, such as the National Collegiate Athletic Association (hereinafter NCAA)"
  — Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn., 7 Cal. 4th 1, 865 P.2d 633 (1994) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1235436/hill-v-national-collegiate-athletic-assn/)
  Known gap: Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. was itself a case about drug testing of NCAA college student-athletes, not employees — its underlying facts don't involve an employer-employee relationship. It is cited here, and by later courts deciding employment drug-testing cases, for the general privacy-claim framework and for this private-party-applicability holding, not because its facts were about a workplace. This document could not independently re-verify Hill's full multi-element framework for evaluating a privacy claim — the specific test a later court applies to weigh a legally protected privacy interest, a reasonable expectation of privacy, and the seriousness of an intrusion against an employer's countervailing interests — against the complete primary opinion text; CourtListener's full-opinion access was rate-limited at the time this document was checked, and only the excerpt quoted above (from a concurring and dissenting opinion describing the majority's conclusion) could be confirmed as an exact quotation. This clause states only that narrower, confirmed point, and should not be read as restating Hill's complete holding or reasoning. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program.

DRUG TESTING TIED TO A NEW POSITION
In Loder v. City of Glendale (1997), the California Supreme Court considered a municipal employer's drug-testing program applied to "all individuals who conditionally have been offered new positions with the city" — a category the court's opinion describes as covering "both newly hired persons and current city employees who have been approved for promotion to a new position", who "are required to undergo urinalysis testing". Because the City of Glendale is a government employer, the case also implicated the Fourth Amendment: as one justice's separate opinion put it, "Mandatory urinalysis drug and alcohol testing of prospective and current employees by a government employer is a search within the scope of the Fourth Amendment." A private employer's testing program, by contrast, doesn't trigger the Fourth Amendment at all — only the state constitutional privacy right described elsewhere in this document can reach it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In this case we address a challenge to an employment-related drug testing program adopted by the City of Glendale in 1986. Under the program in question, all individuals who conditionally have been offered new positions with the city (both newly hired persons and current city employees who have been approved for promotion to a new position) are required to undergo urinalysis testing"
  — Loder v. City of Glendale, 14 Cal. 4th 846, 927 P.2d 1200 (1997) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123039/loder-v-city-of-glendale/)
  "The Fourth Amendment of the United States Constitution protects an individual from unreasonable searches and seizures. Mandatory urinalysis drug and alcohol testing of prospective and current employees by a government employer is a search within the scope of the Fourth Amendment."
  — Loder v. City of Glendale, 14 Cal. 4th 846, 927 P.2d 1200 (1997) (Kennard, J., concurring and dissenting) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123039/loder-v-city-of-glendale/)
  Known gap: The category of testing actually before the court in Loder was testing tied to a conditional offer of a new position — covering both new hires and current employees moving to a new position through promotion — not simply "pre-employment" testing in isolation from "incumbent employee" testing as a strict two-category line. This document could not independently re-verify, against the complete primary opinion text, the specific reasoning the court gave for why that category of testing was upheld, or precisely how the court treated suspicionless testing of an employee who is not moving into a new position; CourtListener's full-opinion access was rate-limited at the time this document was checked, and only the excerpts quoted above could be confirmed as exact quotations from the opinion and a separate concurring and dissenting opinion in the same case. This clause states only those narrower, confirmed points, and should not be read as restating the court's complete holding. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program.

ACCOMMODATING VOLUNTARY REHABILITATION
Separately from drug testing itself, California law requires a private employer that regularly employs 25 or more employees to reasonably accommodate an employee who wants to voluntarily enter and participate in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program, as long as the accommodation doesn't impose an undue hardship on the employer. This duty doesn't protect an employee whose current use of alcohol or drugs leaves them unable to perform their job duties, or unable to perform them without endangering their own health or safety or the health or safety of others — an employer may still refuse to hire, or may discharge, an employee on that basis.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Every private employer regularly employing 25 or more employees shall reasonably accommodate any employee who wishes to voluntarily enter and participate in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program, provided that this reasonable accommodation does not impose an undue hardship on the employer. Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to prohibit an employer from refusing to hire, or discharging an employee who, because of the employee’s current use of alcohol or drugs, is unable to perform his or her duties, or cannot perform the duties in a manner which would not endanger his or her health or safety or the health or safety of others."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1025 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, employer accommodation of voluntary rehabilitation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1025.)
  Known gap: This accommodation duty applies only to a private employer that regularly employs 25 or more employees — smaller employers aren't covered by this chapter of the Labor Code at all. Neither "reasonably accommodate" nor "undue hardship" is defined further within this statute itself. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Other states' accommodation obligations toward an employee entering rehabilitation, if any, differ or may not exist. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program. It does not itself grant or deny any accommodation.

PRIVACY OF ENROLLMENT, PAID LEAVE, AND ENFORCEMENT
The same statutory chapter adds three more rules. An employer must make reasonable efforts to safeguard the privacy of the fact that an employee has enrolled in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program. Nothing in the chapter requires an employer to provide time off with pay for this purpose — but an employee may use their own accrued sick leave to enter and participate in a program. And an employee who believes they've been denied the reasonable accommodation described above may file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner, using the same complaint procedure available for certain other Labor Code claims.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The employer shall make reasonable efforts to safeguard the privacy of the employee as to the fact that he or she has enrolled in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1026 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, privacy of rehabilitation enrollment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1026.)
  "Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to require an employer to provide time off with pay, except that an employee may use sick leave to which he or she is entitled for the purpose of entering and participating in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1027 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, no paid-time-off requirement, sick leave available (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1027.)
  "An employee may file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner if he or she believes that he or she has been denied reasonable accommodation as required by this chapter. Sections 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.4, 98.5, 98.6, and 98.7 shall be applicable to a complaint filed pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1028 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner complaint procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1028.)
  Known gap: Sections 1026, 1027, and 1028 are three different sections of the same narrow, five-section statutory chapter as the accommodation duty in the previous clause (Labor Code §§ 1025-1028) — they are being treated here together as one connected source on a single statutory scheme, not as independent corroborating sources on separate questions. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Other states' rules on privacy of rehabilitation enrollment, paid time off for it, and how a denied accommodation is enforced, if any, differ. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program. It does not itself resolve any complaint about a denied accommodation.

OFF-DUTY CANNABIS USE AND METABOLITE SCREENING
Since January 1, 2024, California law makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against a person in hiring, termination, or any other term or condition of employment based on "the person's use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace," or based on "an employer-required drug screening test that has found the person to have nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites in their hair, blood, urine, or other bodily fluids." The metabolite rule exists because standard urine and hair tests detect nonpsychoactive metabolites that can remain in the body for days or weeks after use — long after any impairment has ended — so a positive result on that kind of test doesn't show current impairment. The law separately makes it unlawful for an employer to ask an applicant about their prior cannabis use. None of this protection applies to an employee in the building and construction trades.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The person’s use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace. This paragraph does not prohibit an employer from discriminating in hiring, or any term or condition of employment, or otherwise penalize a person based on scientifically valid preemployment drug screening conducted through methods that do not screen for nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, off-duty cannabis use protection and preemployment-screening carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "An employer-required drug screening test that has found the person to have nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites in their hair, blood, urine, or other bodily fluids."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, nonpsychoactive-metabolite screening protection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "This subdivision does not apply to an employee in the building and construction trades."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, building and construction trades carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "Except as specified in subdivision (c), it is unlawful for an employer to request information from an applicant for employment relating to the applicant’s prior use of cannabis."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, restriction on asking about prior cannabis use (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  Known gap: The three points above — the off-duty-use protection, the nonpsychoactive-metabolite screening protection, and the building-and-construction-trades carve-out — are all subdivisions of one statutory section, Government Code § 12954(a), and the applicant-inquiry restriction quoted here is subdivision (b) of that same section; all are being treated together as one connected source, not as independent corroborating sources. This protection also has further limits not described in this clause, covered in the next one. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Most other states have no equivalent off-duty-cannabis-use employment protection, and where one exists, the details vary. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program.

LIMITS ON THE CANNABIS PROTECTION
The off-duty cannabis protection described above has specific limits. It doesn't give an employee the right to possess, be impaired by, or use cannabis on the job, and it doesn't affect an employer's rights or obligations to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace. It doesn't preempt any state or federal law that requires applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances — including as a condition of federal funding, federal licensing-related benefits, or a federal contract. And it doesn't apply at all to positions that require a federal government background investigation or security clearance under U.S. Department of Defense regulations, or equivalent regulations of other federal agencies. The statute itself became operative on January 1, 2024.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This section does not permit an employee to possess, to be impaired by, or to use, cannabis on the job, or affect the rights or obligations of an employer to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace, as specified in Section 11362.45 of the Health and Safety Code, or any other rights or obligations of an employer specified by state or federal law or regulation."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, on-the-job use and drug-free workplace carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "This section does not preempt state or federal laws requiring applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances, including laws and regulations requiring applicants or employees to be tested, or the manner in which they are tested, as a condition of employment, receiving federal funding or federal licensing-related benefits, or entering into a federal contract."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, no preemption of federal or state testing requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "This section does not apply to applicants or employees hired for positions that require a federal government background investigation or security clearance in accordance with regulations issued by the United States Department of Defense pursuant to Part 117 of Title 32 of the Code of Federal Regulations, or equivalent regulations applicable to other agencies."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, federal security-clearance positions excluded (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  "This section shall become operative on January 1, 2024."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(g) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, effective date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12954.)
  Known gap: Subdivisions (d), (e), (f), and (g) are all part of the same statutory section as the protection described in the previous clause, Government Code § 12954 — they are being treated together here as one connected source, not as independent corroborating sources. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Cannabis remains a Schedule I controlled substance under the federal Controlled Substances Act, and federal contractors and federally regulated positions can be required to test for it regardless of this state law, exactly as this clause states. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program. It does not determine whether any particular position falls within one of these exemptions.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate that you have received and reviewed this information sheet.

Applicant / Employee: Morgan T. Ellis
Date: _______________

—

This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Most other states have no equivalent off-duty-cannabis-use employment protection, and where one exists, the details vary. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program.

expectedJSON.body: The off-duty cannabis protection described above has specific limits. It doesn't give an employee the right to possess, be impaired by, or use cannabis on the job, and it doesn't affect an employer's rights or obligations to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace. It doesn't preempt any state or federal law that requires applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances — including as a condition of federal funding, federal licensing-related benefits, or a federal contract. And it doesn't apply at all to positions that require a federal government background investigation or security clearance under U.S. Department of Defense regulations, or equivalent regulations of other federal agencies. The statute itself became operative on January 1, 2024.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, on-the-job use and drug-free workplace carve-out
citations.quote: This section does not permit an employee to possess, to be impaired by, or to use, cannabis on the job, or affect the rights or obligations of an employer to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace, as specified in Section 11362.45 of the Health and Safety Code, or any other rights or obligations of an employer specified by state or federal law or regulation.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, no preemption of federal or state testing requirements
citations.quote: This section does not preempt state or federal laws requiring applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances, including laws and regulations requiring applicants or employees to be tested, or the manner in which they are tested, as a condition of employment, receiving federal funding or federal licensing-related benefits, or entering into a federal contract.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, federal security-clearance positions excluded
citations.quote: This section does not apply to applicants or employees hired for positions that require a federal government background investigation or security clearance in accordance with regulations issued by the United States Department of Defense pursuant to Part 117 of Title 32 of the Code of Federal Regulations, or equivalent regulations applicable to other agencies.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: This section shall become operative on January 1, 2024.

expectedJSON.gap: Subdivisions (d), (e), (f), and (g) are all part of the same statutory section as the protection described in the previous clause, Government Code § 12954 — they are being treated together here as one connected source, not as independent corroborating sources. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Cannabis remains a Schedule I controlled substance under the federal Controlled Substances Act, and federal contractors and federally regulated positions can be required to test for it regardless of this state law, exactly as this clause states. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program. It does not determine whether any particular position falls within one of these exemptions.
